items.title: Observe an approved root specimen
items.student: Teacher supplies a healthy pre-grown seedling with roots supported moist on a tray and an approved hand lens. Observe without pulling/root cutting. Draw only visible root features and label root hairs only if resolved;record specimen,tool and an observation limit. Use supplied conceptual description separately:many young absorbing regions bear thin root-hair extensions that increase contact with soil water. No assumed microscopic detail from an unaided view.
items.teacher: Teacher prepares seedlings days beforehand,checks species/sap allergies and hygiene;no mouldy cultures/unknown toxic plants/soil aerosols. Actual observable root/branch/hair detail depends on sample and lens;NOTSEEN does not mean absent. Model root hairs increase absorbing area/shorten distance to membrane;visible morphology alone does not demonstrate ion transport mechanism. Clean hands and trays after use.

items.title: Water and ions need different explanations
items.student: Conceptual cases,not measured plant data:Asoil has higher water potential than root cell under suitable conditions;Broot cells accumulate an essential ion against its concentration gradient;Csoil solution becomes very concentrated. Explain water entry,possible energy-dependent ion uptake and a reason excess dissolved salts may hinder water uptake. Draw labelled soil→root→xylem pathway and distinguish a water-potential gradient from an ion-concentration gradient.
items.teacher: Water crosses selectively permeable cell membranes by osmosis down water potential under stated conditions;ion uptake uses selective transporters,with energy-dependent uptake possible against gradients. Not every ion movement is always active. Mineral ions are not food/sugars and do not enter by osmosis. Concentrated soil can lower water potential and reduce/reverse entry. Root pathways ultimately supply xylem;avoid claiming every water molecule crosses every cortex cell membrane.

items.title: Cohesion,adhesion and transpiration pull
items.student: Use this supplied mechanism model:water evaporates from moist leaf cell-wall surfaces,vapour diffuses through stomatal openings,and tension is transmitted through connected xylem water. Explain how cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to walls support the column. Compare with a teacher-approved digital transport model;record what you actually viewed and one model limit. If no device,use this printed model and mark actual digital viewing NOT OBSERVED.
items.teacher: Cohesion/adhesion support water columns;evaporation and water-potential gradients generate a transpiration pull. Capillarity alone is not a complete explanation for tall-tree ascent;no claim leaves pump by muscular action. Root pressure may contribute in some conditions but is not the sole general driver. Digital animation is a representation,not an observation of the learner’s specimen. No water experiments with electricity.

items.title: Source and sink can change
items.student: Draw two labelled source→phloem→sink models:(1)mature photosynthesising leaf supplying growing roots and shoot tip;(2)sprouting storage organ supplying developing shoot before its leaves photosynthesise sufficiently. Explain why phloem transport need not always point downward. State the role of sugars,loading/unloading,water and pressure differences without treating all loading strategies as identical.
items.teacher: Sucrose/other organic solutes travel in living phloem from source to sink;different tubes/routes may carry in different directions simultaneously. Stored reserves can make a tuber/bulb a source and a developing organ a sink;roles change. Loading/unloading and water movement contribute to pressure-driven bulk flow;energy may be used in loading/maintenance,not a tiny pump at every segment. Xylem water/mineral transport differs;phloem also contains water.

items.title: What evidence tests a phloem model?
items.student: Research context:Knoblauch and colleagues(2016),Testing the Münch hypothesis of long distance phloem transport in plants,eLife5:e15341,DOI10.7554/eLife.15341. The researchers combined pressure,flow and anatomical resistance measurements in morning glory to test whether pressure-driven transport was physically plausible. This short account gives no copied numerical result. Separately consider fictional teaching evidence:labelled sugar appears in sinks connected by intact phloem,whereas an interrupted phloem path changes its arrival. What is supported,and which alternative damage/source effects need controls? Does coloured water in xylem prove sugar translocation?
items.teacher: Primary research DOIhttps://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.15341;abstract/archive search evidence supports this narrow design description,not a claim all transport questions were settled. Fictional tracer case supports a phloem-path association with suitable sham/healthy controls,not direct proof from colour or uncontrolled injury. Coloured water usually illustrates a water route,not organic sugar phloem translocation. No learner ring-barking,radioactive tracer,aphid handling or destructive sap sampling;research interpretation is not performed phloem experimentation. Background physiologyhttps://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/30-5-transport-of-water-and-solutes-in-plants;use qualified statements because some textbook absolutes are overgeneralised.

items.title: Plan a mass-loss investigation
items.student: Teacher prepares stable leafy-shoot mass potometers:each safe plastic water vessel is sealed around the shoot and every exposed water surface is sealed,leaves dry;a matched sealed vessel without shoot tests background mass loss/leaks. Teacher alone cuts/assembles supports shoots and keeps all electronics dry. Plan airflow comparison and a separate structural-area comparison. Record start/end mass(g),duration(min),background loss,conditions,leaf-area proxy,replicateID and named actions. Explain why mass loss and bubble displacement measure different quantities.
items.teacher: Primary method contexthttps://www.saps.org.uk/teaching-resources/resources/1263/investigating-transpiration-with-a-potometer/ distinguishes mass loss and bubble water uptake,and recommends technician assembly. This is an independently specified low-risk mass-loss design;teacher must pilot actual plant/balance sensitivity,seals and duration. Net mass loss mainly reflects water loss over short runs with negligible other mass exchange,not exact transpiration under every condition. Bubble potometer records uptake as proxy;distance/time is not itself water volume. No untested equipment is assumed ready.

items.title: Perform an environmental-factor comparison
items.student: With teacher-approved preassembled mass potometers,compare still air with gentle hand-fan airflow for10minutes using similar shoots and sealed no-shoot backgrounds. Keep light,temperature,humidity,duration,starting hydration and leaf-area proxy as comparable as possible;record remaining differences. Take actual start/end masses on a dry stable balance away from drafts;stop fan during each weighing. Use at least3replicates per condition across class groups and retain raw values. Each learner performs a named weighing/timing/recording/check action. Do not invent the expected direction if change is too small.
items.teacher: Teacher pilots10minute detectability and supplies sufficient matched equipment/backgrounds;extend session/opportunities if necessary,not fabricate data. Hand fan keeps electricity away from water;standardise distance/cadence and acknowledge airflow not calibrated. Compute netloss=(start-end)-backgroundloss,rate/netduration. Positive netloss under fan often supports greater water loss under measured conditions;humidity/water-stress/stomatal responses may differ. Class replicates are not automatically independent if same shoot reused;report design. Demonstration/supplied values cannot certify individual investigation.

items.title: Perform a structural leaf-area comparison
items.student: Use teacher-prepared comparable shoots with full leaf area versus reduced area;teacher removes selected leaves before class and seals/standardises cut sites where appropriate. Keep hydration,time,ambient conditions,shoottype and setup comparable;trace remaining leaf outlines on squared paper for one-sided area proxy. Collect10minute mass losses and sealed no-shoot backgrounds,at least3replicates per condition across class. Record actual named actions and compare total loss plus rate per area if areas known. Identify a confound from plant variation,wounding or time rather than calling this a perfect isolated test.
items.teacher: Leaf area is a structural factor;larger area can support more total water loss when other factors comparable. One-sided outline is a stated proxy,not exact full stomatal surface;donot silently double and treat both sides equivalent. Reduced-leaf pairedshoot design can confound size/wounding/physiology;use replicates/randomised assignment and report limits. Teacher does all cutting;no blades/pupil sap exposure. Teacher pilots sensitivity and may extend timing;unperformed actions NOTOBSERVED. Separate this from environmental comparison rather than interpreting uncontrolled leaf differences as pure airflow effect.

items.title: Calculate and limit supplied results
items.student: Fictional teaching runs,not your observations:over10min,still-air shoot losses0.20,0.22,0.18g;fan-shoot losses0.35,0.37,0.36g;backgroundloss0.02g for each run. Calculate mean corrected losses and g/min rates. Separate structural fictional pair:area40cm²,netloss0.20g versusarea20cm²,netloss0.10g over10min. Compare total loss and rate/cm². Explain how light,humidity,temperature,stomatal aperture,cuticle or leaf area may affect loss without claiming all responses are universally monotonic.
items.teacher: Correctedstill0.18,0.20,0.16g,mean0.18g,rate0.018g/min;fan0.33,0.35,0.34g,mean0.34g,rate0.034g/min. Fan association in this fictional controlled comparison,not realclass evidence. Structural rates0.02and0.01g/min,each0.0005g/(mincm²). Moretotal area neednot higher per-area rate. Higher humidity often reduces vapour gradient;light/heat/air movement responses depend on stomata/water supply. If background large/drifting,repeat/check leaks;negative corrected loss is uncertainty/failure evidence,not forced positive transpiration.

items.title: Water transport supports life but has costs
items.student: Explain how transpiration-linked transport supplies water/mineral movement,cooling and tissue hydration while excessive loss can cause wilting/stomatal closure and reduce carbon uptake. Prepare a short checked awareness message for a teacher-approved class/school audience on appropriate watering and nutrient management. Name source-listed fertilisers DAP,CAN,urea as nutrient sources,not plant food or universal cures. Explain why soil/plant need,label/local expert guidance and avoiding runoff/overapplication matter. Do not handle fertilisers/manure or give dose prescriptions.
items.teacher: Use transport reasoning and one explicit benefit/limit. Fertilisers provide mineral nutrients rather than replacing photosynthesis;organic manure needs safe managed use. Concentrated salts/runoff can harm plants/environment;watering also must fit conditions,not constant flooding. Teacher reviews the message and arranges any actual class/school sharing;record named presentation/contribution,not claim community impact. No automatic external messages or chemical handling. Source suggested communityawareness is adapted through approved classroom audience;actual community engagement remains teacher confirmation.

items.title: Audit transport claims
items.student: Correct:(1)roots absorb sugars as mineral food by osmosis;(2)phloem flows only down;(3)bubble speed directly equals transpiration volume;(4)coloured water proves sugar transport;(5)all plants should always maximise water loss;(6)reading supplied mass data proves you performed the experiment. For each give a corrected mechanism/evidence limit and link one correction to a useful watering/nutrient message.
items.teacher: Ion uptake differs from osmosis and plant photosynthate food;phloemsource/sinkroutescanpointdifferentdirections;bubblespeedrequirescrosssection/uptake assumptions andisnotdirectevaporationvolume;dyedxylemrouteisnotsugarphloem;waterlossbenefits/risksmustbalance;performedactionneedsactualobservation. A specific supported benefit may evidence reasoned appreciation,not lasting attitude. No reagent/clinical recommendation.

items.title: Independent transport evidence sheet
items.student: Fictional FinalA mass-potometer runs,last10minutes:still-air shoot losses0.16,0.18,0.17g;gentle-airflow shoot losses0.28,0.30,0.29g;each matched sealed background loses0.01g. FinalB:stored reserves supply a sprouting shoot before sufficient leaf photosynthesis;later mature leaves supply developing roots. These data are not your actual observations. Use only this sheet and final questions.
